UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms                      )                Docket No. AD26-7-000

                   COMMENTS OF FIRSTENERGY SERVICE COMPANY

        Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) July 30, 2026,

Notice Requesting Post Conference Comments on PJM governance and stakeholder processes, 1

FirstEnergy Service Company (“FirstEnergy”) 2 respectfully submits the following comments.

        I.       INTRODUCTION

        The key proposition that prompted the July Technical Conference is that PJM

Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”)’s governance and stakeholder process is not able to address

system needs in a “timely and efficient manner.” 3 This, however, is an incomplete characterization

of the present challenges to the PJM system. The central problem in the PJM region is not

governance itself; it is a shortage of generation needed to ensure resource adequacy. PJM

governance reforms may improve efficiency, but they will not, by themselves, produce any

additional generation capacity. Therefore, while FirstEnergy supports effectively tailored reforms

to PJM governance, FirstEnergy believes that the most important reforms are improving the

interconnection framework and enhancing state level coordination, in order to enable PJM and the

         II.      RESOURCE ADEQUACY AND INADEQUATE CAPACITY ARE THE
                  CENTRAL CHALLENGE

                  A. The Current Resource Adequacy Challenge in the PJM Footprint Is Not
                     the Result of Poor Governance.

         As the Commission and industry have recognized, electric load demand is outpacing supply

at an unprecedented rate due to the rise in new large loads interconnection requests. 4 Further

compounding the challenge is the premature retirement of existing generation and the delayed rate

of entry of new generation resources. 5 This mismatch between rapidly increasing demand and

inadequate generation supply is the preeminent threat to grid reliability and affordability.

         Peak demand in PJM is projected to increase dramatically, driven largely by data center

growth. 6 At the same time, state policies have accelerated retirements of existing dispatchable

generation. Since 2015, PJM has seen over 34 GW of generation retire. 7 Even with PJM’s

interconnection queue reforms, the region still needs new dispatchable generation. Although PJM

has the authority to administer markets, plan transmission, and operate the transmission system,

PJM does not have the authority to compel or otherwise direct the construction of generation

resources. 8 For that reason, governance reform alone cannot solve the capacity shortage.

         The need to attract more megawatts is not unique to PJM. RTOs and ISOs across the

country face similar pressure from rapid load growth, including data center development, and

accelerated retirements driven by energy transition policies. 9 Better governance in PJM may

improve process efficiency, but it will not materially change PJM’s supply/demand imbalance.

Simply put, PJM governance did not cause the capacity shortage, and governance reform alone

cannot produce the generation needed to solve the resource adequacy challenge.

                 B. PJM Governance Reform Will Not Solve the Missing Megawatt Problem.

        Section 201 of the Federal Power Act reserves to the states the authority over generation

development, siting, and resource adequacy. 10 While PJM has limited tools to support resource

adequacy, including administering markets to produce price signals and curtailment mechanisms,

under the cooperative federalism framework, ultimate direct authority over resource adequacy

rests with the states. Thus, only the states have the authority to dictate whether sufficient generation

is built on a timely basis.

        The PJM interconnection queue reforms have done little to add new capacity to the system.

As a result, capacity prices for the two most recent Base Residual Auctions cleared at or near the

administrative cap producing record high prices. 11 Yet PJM still faces regionwide reliability

concerns tied to insufficient new generation resources. As such, PJM governance is not the sole

constraint. The solution therefore must include state level action and state policy reforms that

account for large load growth and remove barriers to entry for new generation including permitting

 delays, local siting restrictions, financing challenges, equipment shortages and physical

constraints.

        The PJM governance reforms discussed during the July 23 technical conference, including

Board authority, nominating committee composition, stakeholder processes, state participation,

and filing rights, do not answer the central question: who will build new generation, and how will

it be adequately incentivized? The states must bridge the gap between the growing energy needs

of large loads and the state policies that have encouraged generation retirements or created barriers

to generation development.

                C. PJM’s Diverse Footprint is Distinct from Neighboring RTOs/ISOs and
                   Contributes to both Resource Adequacy and Governance Challenges.

        There is no question that the states have the primary role in ensuring resource adequacy

and have a significant influence on PJM governance. How that influence is exercised, however,

raises complex and important considerations. The Commission should consider the noteworthy

variation across PJM when compared to other RTO regions. The geographic footprint of PJM

covers all or part of thirteen states and the District of Columbia. Those jurisdictions do not share

a single energy policy, regulatory structure, or resource adequacy model. PJM includes both

vertically integrated and restructured states, and its states have different generation policies, retail

structures, load growth profiles, resource adequacy preferences, and political priorities. Those

differences have affected regional infrastructure development and resource adequacy, including

through generation retirements.

        This diversity makes PJM materially different from RTOs/ISOs in which state engagement

can be represented by a shared, or at least substantially similar, set of state policies. The

coordination required to reach state consensus in PJM on complex market and transmission

planning issues would likely further delay efforts to bring new generation resources online. The

                                                   4
 Commission therefore should not assume that state governance models used in other RTOs/ISOs

can be transplanted into PJM without creating new opportunities for deadlock, gamesmanship, or

inconsistent regional outcomes. The states in PJM need to enhance coordination among their

public utility commissions, state administrations, and other relevant state authorities such as the

Organization of PJM States, Inc. ("OPSI”) and the Consumer Advocates of the PJM States

(“CAPS”) so that the states have a more cohesive and effective voice in the PJM stakeholder

process.

        III.    THE COST OF ADDRESSING THE RESOURCE ADEQUACY
                CHALLENGE SHOULD NOT FALL TO EXISTING CUSTOMERS

                A. Existing Customers Are Bearing the Costs of the Growing Resource
                   Adequacy Challenge.

        FirstEnergy recognizes the importance of protecting existing customers from dramatic cost

increases caused by the growth of data centers and new large loads. As the supply and demand

imbalance persists, the costs increasingly appear in consumer bills. Despite soaring capacity

auction prices which resulted in all-time high clearing prices or the market cap in multiple auctions,

consumers have paid $16 billion with minimal new generation resulting. 12 The Commission should

focus any reforms on solutions that will equip PJM with the ability to implement solutions that

improve reliability and mitigate the costs customers are now shouldering.

        The Commission should not rely solely on governance reforms to protect customers from

increased rates and reliability risks caused by the ongoing resource adequacy challenge. As

explained above, the most effective solution will require state level changes that support the

development of and investment in new dispatchable generation.




12
       PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 2027/2028 Base Residual Auction Results Report (Dec. 17, 2025) (reporting
an RTO clearing price of $333.44/MW-day and total capacity costs of approximately $16.4 billion).
                                                     5
                B. New Large Load Customers Should Be Required to Bring the Generation
                  Necessary to Serve Their Load or Take Service Through a Reliability
                  Backstop Procurement Mechanism.

       New large loads, including data centers, are driving much of the unprecedented growth in

electric demand. Under longstanding cost causation principles, the cost of meeting that demand

should be borne by the new large loads, not existing customers. As the Commission considers

appropriate reforms to address the resource adequacy challenge, the central focus of any solution

must be to bring more generation online.

       A bring-your-own-generation construct protects existing customers from subsidizing new

large loads while helping bring new generation online. Alternatively, new large loads that do not

bring their own generation should take service through a targeted reliability backstop procurement

construct. That backstop would secure the resources needed to meet increased demand and

maintain system reliability.

       The current framework both raises affordability concerns and worsens the resource

adequacy challenge. New large loads that materially increase system demand should be expected

either to bring adequate supply resources or bear the costs of procuring adequate additional

generation necessary to support their demand. Under the status quo interconnection framework,

new large loads will continue to adversely impact existing customers that are currently absorbing

the increasing costs of generation. A construct that requires that new large loads either bring their

own generation or bear the costs of targeted reliability backstop procurement better aligns cost

responsibility with cost causation and mitigates adverse impacts on existing customers.

               C. Generation Procured for Native Load Growth Should Flow Through a
                  Pass-Through Tariff.

       FirstEnergy supports a framework that ensures the customer causing the need for or

benefiting from the availability of increased generation bears the costs. The Commission should

                                                 6
 further consider reforms that allow costs to serve native load growth, separate from new large load

demand, to flow through to native-load customers through a pass-through tariff.

       Consistent with cost causation principles, once a state, utility, or other responsible entity

determines that new generation must be procured to serve native load growth, distinct from large

load growth, the associated costs should be recovered through a transparent pass-through tariff.

Under a pass-through tariff, a state-regulated utility would recover the prudently incurred costs of

generation resources procured to serve incremental native-load growth through a dedicated retail

rider charged to the customers benefiting from that procurement. The rider would permit periodic

recovery of capacity, generation, and associated resource adequacy costs and would align cost

responsibility with the customers whose load growth necessitated the new generation investment.

Such a tariff would reduce the risk that customers not causing the need for or benefiting from the

new capacity procurement subsidize resources procured for incremental native load growth.

               D. FirstEnergy Supports Resource Adequacy Solutions that Assign Costs to
                  the Customers Driving the Demand or Benefiting from the New
                  Generation.

       FirstEnergy shares the Commission’s goal of ensuring that customers have timely and

efficient access to adequate, affordable, and reliable service. To meet that goal, FirstEnergy

continues to support a transmission expansion framework that promotes affordability by requiring

large load customers pay an expansion rate designed to recover network upgrade costs needed to

support their interconnection.

       This framework requires the large load driving new demand to bear the cost of

interconnection and associated network upgrades. It also reduces costs to existing customers while

preserving operational benefits for all customers.      FirstEnergy submitted in the large load




                                                 7
 rulemaking docket a whitepaper providing an overview of how a rate expansion framework would

be designed, and anticipates providing further details on this proposal in the near future. 13

       IV.     GOVERNANCE REFORMS SHOULD BE LIMITED TO REFORMS
               THAT IMPROVE EFFICIENCY WHILE RESPECTING EXISTING
               JURISDICTIONAL AND CONTRACTUAL BOUNDARIES

       FirstEnergy agrees that PJM governance is important and warrants Commission attention,

particularly because efficient decision-making is needed to address the resource adequacy

challenge threatening affordability and reliability. If the Commission directs reforms to PJM

governance or the stakeholder process, those reforms should be targeted and should not diminish

the rights and responsibilities established under the Consolidated Transmission Owners

Agreement (“CTOA”), which is the foundational agreement that created and defines PJM’s

authority over regional transmission planning and operation.

       FirstEnergy supports limited reforms to the PJM governance structure in three respects.

First, FirstEnergy recommends that the stakeholder process be reformed to assume a purely

advisory role in PJM governance. Second, FirstEnergy recommends that the states be given formal

standing at PJM with a defined right to bring issues directly to the Board. Finally, PJM governance

reform should respect both the jurisdictional divide between the Commission and the states and

the balance of rights and obligations between PJM and PJM transmission owners established under

the CTOA.

       FirstEnergy recommends that the stakeholder process transition to an advisory vote

approach that is less capable of producing prolonged deadlock. The reformed process would follow

a course under which PJM would develop proposals, those proposals would be subject to

stakeholder discussion and advice, and the Board would then, with the benefit of stakeholder input,



13
       Supplemental Comments of FirstEnergy Service Company, Docket No. RM26-4-000 (June 5, 2026).
                                                   8
 determine what to file at the Commission for acceptance. The PJM Board should be the final

decision-maker on solutions to issues that are within the authority of the Board under the PJM

governing documents including the CTOA. This streamlined process would retain PJM Board

accountability while enabling quicker decision-making.

          FirstEnergy also recommends an enhanced role for states with a more meaningful “seat at

the table.” States currently have only a limited role in PJM governance despite the fact that they

have primary authority over resource adequacy and transmission siting. States need a formal

governance role rather than soft influence through fragmented OPSI interactions and one-off

communications. The PJM governance structure must incorporate meaningful input from the PJM

states. In order to provide the States with greater access to the PJM Board, the States should have

formal standing at PJM, and a defined right to bring issues directly to the Board. Participation at

formal meetings with the Board will give States greater access and will improve accountability

and responsiveness.

          As a threshold consideration to PJM governance reform, it is material to recall that the

CTOA is the cornerstone upon which PJM obtained the authority to operate as an RTO. Any

modification to the PJM governance rules must consider the implications for the division of rights

and obligations established under the CTOA. An essential and exclusive right of the PJM

Transmission Owners is the FPA section 205 filing rights over transmission rates and rate design,

including local and regional rates. 14 Moreover, because FPA Section 205 grants filing rights to

“public utilities,” independent Section 205 filing authority cannot be granted to the states absent a

statutory amendment by Congress. Consistent with the Federal Power Act, the CTOA assigns

section 205 rights and responsibilities to PJM and the Transmission Owners—both jurisdictional


14
          CTOA, Article 5, § 5.4, “Federal Power Act Rights”; Article 7, § 7.1, “Individual Transmission Owner
Rates.”
                                                       9
 public utilities—and courts have repeatedly recognized that FERC cannot compel utilities to

surrender those rights or transfer them to non-jurisdictional entities. 15 As such, the Commission

should not accept any reform proposal that would in any way violate or impinge upon the balance

of rights and obligations established under the CTOA.

        V.       CONCLUSION

        For the reasons set forth above, FirstEnergy respectfully urges the Commission to issue an

order that: (i) recognizes resource adequacy, not governance alone, as the central challenge facing

PJM; (ii) directs PJM to pursue targeted governance reforms that improve efficiency while

preserving CTOA rights; (iii) directs PJM to develop mechanisms under which new large loads

either bring generation or bear the costs of reliability backstop procurement; and (iv) directs PJM

to make a compliance filing proposing tariff revisions consistent with those principles.
